title: Oracles of demons and the risen Jesus
source_text: Οὐ χρεία τοίνυν ἡμῖν ὡς οὕτω ζητοῦσι τὸν θεὸν ἀπιέναι, ὅπου ἡμᾶς πέμπει ὁ Κέλσος, εἰς Τροφωνίου καὶ εἰς Ἀμφιάρεω καὶ εἰς Μόψου, ἔνθα φησὶν ἀνθρωποειδεῖς θεωρεῖσθαι θεοὺς καὶ, ὡς λέγει Κέλσος, οὐ ψευδομένους ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐναργεῖς. ἴσμεν γὰρ ἡμεῖς τούτους δαίμονας ὄντας, τρεφομένους κνίσσαις καὶ αἵμασι καὶ ταῖς ἀπὸ τῶν θυσιῶν ἀναθυμιάσεσι καὶ οὕτω παρακατεχομένους ἐν τοῖς ἀπὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν κατασκευασθεῖσι δεσμωτηρίοις· ἅτινα ἱερὰ θεῶν Ἕλληνες νενομίκασιν. ἀλλ᾿ ἡμεῖς ἴσμεν ἀπατεώνων δαιμόνων εἶναι τὰ τοιαῦτα οἰκητήρια. μετὰ ταῦτα κακοήθως ὁ Κέλσος φησὶ περὶ τῶν προειρημένων ἀνθρωποειδῶν κατ᾿ αὐτὸν θεῶν ὅτι ὄψεταί τις αὐτοὺς οὐχ ἅπαξ παραῤῥυέντας ὥσπερ τὸν τούτους ἐξαπατήσαντα ἀλλ᾿ ἀεὶ τοῖς βουλομένοις ὁμιλοῦντας. καὶ ἔοικέ γε διὰ τούτων φάσμα μὲν νενομικέναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν, μετὰ τὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀνάστασιν ἐπιφανέντα τοῖς μαθηταῖς, ὡσπερεὶ παραῤῥεύσαντα πρὸς τὸ ὀφθῆναι αὐτοῖς· οὕς δ᾿ ὠνόμασε λέγων ἀνθρωποειδεῖς θεοὺς, τούτους οἴεται ἀεὶ τοῖς βουλομένοις ὁμιλεῖν. πῶς δὲ δύναται φάσμα, ὥς φησιν αὐτὸς, παραῤῥυὲν ἐπ᾿ ἀπάτῃ τῶν θεασαμένων καὶ μετὰ τὴν τότε ὄψιν τοσαῦτα ἐνεργεῖν καὶ ἐπιστρέφειν τὰς τῶν τοιούτων ψυχὰς καὶ πειθὼ ἐμποιεῖν αὐταῖς περὶ τοῦ πάντα δεῖν ἀρεσκόντως πράττειν θεῷ ὡς κριθησομένους; πῶς δὲ φάσμα ὀνομασθὲν ἀπελαύνει δαιμόνια καὶ ἄλλας οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτους ἐνεργείας ἐνεργεῖ, οὐχ ἕνα κεκληρωμένον τόπον ὡς οἱ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν ἀνθρωποειδεῖς θεοὶ ἀλλὰ διῆκον ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην καὶ συνάγον καὶ ἕλκον τῇ ἑαυτοῦ θειότητι οὓς ἂν εὕροι πρὸς τὸν καλὸν βίον κλίναντας ἑαυτούς;
pass_a_gloss: No need (χρεία) for us, as so seeking (ζητέω) God, to go away (ἄπειμι) where Celsus sends (πέμπω) us, to (the shrines of) Trophonius, Amphiaraus, Mopsus, where he says human-shaped (ἀνθρωποειδής) gods are beheld (θεωρέω), and, as Celsus says, not lying (ψεύδομαι) but even manifest (ἐναργής). For we know these are demons (δαίμων), nourished (τρέφω) by savour of fat (κνῖσα), bloods (αἷμα), the exhalations (ἀναθυμίασις) from sacrifices (θυσία), and so held fast (παρακατέχω) in prisons (δεσμωτήριον) constructed (κατασκευάζω) from their desire (ἐπιθυμία); which the Greeks have reckoned (νομίζω) temples (ἱερόν) of gods. But we know such are dwellings (οἰκητήριον) of deceiving (ἀπατεών) demons. After this Celsus maliciously (κακοήθως) says of the aforesaid human-shaped gods (according to him) that one will see them not once slipping by (παραρρέω) like the one who deceived (ἐξαπατάω) these, but always conversing (ὁμιλέω) with those who wish. He seems by this to have thought Jesus a phantom (φάσμα), appearing (ἐπιφαίνομαι) to the disciples after resurrection (ἀνάστασις) from the dead, as if slipping by so as to be seen; those he named human-shaped gods he thinks always converse with the willing. How can a phantom, as he says, slipping by for deception (ἀπάτη) of the viewers, even after the sight (ὄψις) then, effect (ἐνεργέω) so much, turn (ἐπιστρέφω) the souls of such, and produce persuasion (πειθώ) in them about needing to do all things pleasingly (ἀρεσκόντως) to God as about to be judged (κρίνω)? How does what is named a phantom drive out (ἀπελαύνω) demons (δαιμόνιον) and work other not-easily-despised workings (ἐνέργεια), not having been allotted (κληρόω) one place as his human-shaped gods, but pervading (διήκω) the whole inhabited world (οἰκουμένη), gathering (συνάγω) and drawing (ἕλκω) by its own divinity (θειότης) whomever it finds having inclined (κλίνω) themselves to the good life (καλὸς βίος)?
pass_b_english: We have no need, then, since we seek God in this way, to go off where Celsus sends us, to Trophonius, to Amphiaraus and to Mopsus, where he says gods in human form are to be seen, and, as Celsus puts it, “not deceptive but even plainly visible.” For we know that these are demons, fed on the savour of burnt fat, on blood, and on the fumes that rise from the sacrifices, and so held fast in prisons built from their own craving; these the Greeks have taken to be temples of gods. But we know that such places are the dwellings of deceiving demons.

After this Celsus speaks with malice about the gods in human form already mentioned, as he calls them, saying that one will see them “not slipping by once, like the one who deceived these people, but always conversing with any who wish.” By these words he seems to have thought that Jesus, who appeared to his disciples after his resurrection from the dead, was a phantom, as though he had slipped by in order to be seen by them; while those he named gods in human form he supposes to converse always with any who wish.

But how can a phantom which, as he himself says, slipped by to deceive those who saw it, go on after that sight to accomplish so much, to turn the souls of such people, and to persuade them that they must do everything in a way pleasing to God, as men who will be judged? And how does what he calls a phantom drive out demons and perform other works not to be despised, not confined to one allotted place, as his gods in human form are, but reaching through the whole inhabited world, and by its own divinity gathering and drawing all whom it finds to have turned themselves toward the good life?

choices.choice: Trophonius (Lebadea), Amphiaraus (Oropus) and Mopsus (Mallus) are oracle-shrines Celsus named in the preceding fragment; the Greek here gives only the names, so no places are added in the English. Celsus’s words are given partly in indirect speech (‘ἔνθα φησὶν ἀνθρωποειδεῖς θεωρεῖσθαι θεοὺς’); only the phrases framed as his (‘οὐ ψευδομένους ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐναργεῖς’; ‘οὐχ ἅπαξ παραρρυέντας ... ὁμιλοῦντας’) are put in quotation marks. παραρρέω (‘flow past, slip by’) is Celsus’s sneer that Jesus’ risen appearance was a fleeting apparition; rendered ‘slipping by’ throughout to keep Origen’s repetition of the word. ‘ὡς κριθησομένους’ rendered ‘as men who will be judged’. Possible echo of Colossians 1:10 in ‘ἀρεσκόντως πράττειν θεῷ’, too loose to cite inline. The subject of the closing participles (διῆκον, συνάγον, ἕλκον) is the neuter φάσμα, i.e. Jesus as Celsus names him; rendered ‘it’ to keep Origen’s ironic grammar, and kept inside the question as in the Greek. ‘κλίναντας ἑαυτούς’ is reflexive: those who have turned themselves toward the good life.
τοίνυν restored ('then') and opening put in Greek order
'that their own craving has built for them' trimmed to 'built from their own craving' (no added 'for them')
closing statement put back inside the question, as in the Greek
κλίναντας ἑαυτούς: 'inclined toward' changed to 'have turned themselves toward' (reflexive agency)
ἐνεργείας ἐνεργεῖ: 'work other works' changed to 'perform other works'
'those who wish' changed to 'any who wish' for natural English
